demographic_context.context_note: Millennial first-time homeowners (2014-2018 purchase) inheriting appliances installed by previous owners (~2010-2015). These represent typical minimum-to-mid-range units chosen by sellers, not premium efficiency investments.

water_rate.calculation: Water Tier 2: $5.83/1000 gal + Wastewater: $7.28/1000 gal = $13.11/1000 gal

source.note: Cobb County 2025 rates; Tier 2 (4,000-15,000 gal/month) typical for 2,000 sq ft home using ~5,000 gal/month; excludes $8 monthly base charge

replacement_logic.explanation: Models real-world behavioral pattern (replacing at failure) with deterministic timing at expected lifespan. People know when appliances are getting old but wait until failure rather than replacing proactively.
replacement_logic.conservative_assumption: Real-world emergency replacements cost 20-30% more (rush fees, limited shopping time, contractor markup), but we model same cost at expected lifespan. This conservative assumption strengthens the thesis - if deterministic replacement shows a replacement trap, emergency replacement (higher cost, potentially earlier failure) would show worse outcomes.
sources: HomeAdvisor: Emergency HVAC replacement costs 15-25% more than planned
Angi: Water heater emergency replacement premium ~20-30%
Consumer Reports: Most homeowners replace appliances at failure, not proactively

appliance_baselines.notes: Represents a standard mid-range 2015 dishwasher (~$550 purchase price, $950 installed in 2025 USD). Energy use (280 kWh/year) reflects midrange non-ENERGY STAR units; efficient models in 2015 achieved 230–250 kWh.
Represents a standard 50-gallon electric resistance tank from 2015, replaced in 2025. Annual energy use ~4,500 kWh.

Represents a standard 3-ton SEER 13 split system installed in 2012 and replaced in 2025. Lifespan of 13 years reflects older system, harder climate (Atlanta), and typical maintenance patterns. Baseline set to 4,000 kWh/year as conservative estimate accounting for typical building envelope deficiencies in homes purchased 2014-2018, consistent with DOE Zone 3A data adjusted for aging housing stock (~11% above typical 3,800 kWh/year for standard Atlanta home). ASHRAE median for residential split systems is 15 years.
Represents whole-home incandescent/halogen usage at ~1,650 kWh/year; lifespan derived from average use (5 hrs/day) and 1,000-hour bulb ratings.
Represents attic with low/no insulation; 4,500 kWh/year HVAC load assumed based on DOE Zone 3A. Post-upgrade values use ~8.9% HVAC energy reduction (400 kWh/year savings).

Category 1: Dishwashers.Notes: Whirlpool and Bosch each include 1-year warranties. Miele includes 2-year full coverage, extendable.
Category 1: Dishwashers.Installation_Cost_Methodology: Installed costs estimated as purchase_price × 1.5-1.6 multiplier (typical for dishwasher installation including removal, plumbing connections, and basic electrical). Whirlpool: $600 × 1.58 = $950; Bosch: $1000 × 1.5 = $1500; Miele: $2000 × 1.5 = $3000. Based on typical Atlanta-area installation costs for standard dishwasher replacement.

Category 3: Air Conditioning - Atlanta.Notes: Represents typical Atlanta installation patterns. Premium mini-splits have highest efficiency but limited ducted retrofits.
Category 3: Air Conditioning - Atlanta.Installation_Cost_Methodology: Installed costs are provided as total installed costs (unit + labor + materials + ductwork where applicable) for Atlanta-area installations. Goodman: $9,750 (baseline SEER 14 minimum, includes ductwork); Trane: $12,000 (premium variable-speed, includes ductwork); Mitsubishi: $7,000 (mini-split, lower due to no ductwork required). Cost ranges validated against: (1) Guardian Experts Atlanta HVAC cost guide (https://guardianexperts.com/blog/what-should-a-new-heating-and-air-system-cost-in-atlanta) - reports $8,000-$15,000 for 3-ton systems; (2) Angi Atlanta AC installation guide (https://www.angi.com/articles/how-much-does-installing-new-ac-cost/ga/atlanta) - reports $3,500-$7,500 for unit only, $6,000-$12,000 installed; (3) Atlanta News First 2025 report (https://www.atlantanewsfirst.com/2025/05/29/replacing-your-air-conditioner-is-more-expensive-than-ever/) - notes rising costs. Selected costs represent mid-range of these sources for 3-ton systems in 2,000 sq ft homes, reflecting 2025 pricing. All costs include full installation (removal, unit, labor, materials, ductwork where applicable, permits).

Models.annual_kWh_calculation: 1,650 kWh baseline (incandescent) – 330 kWh post-retrofit LED = 1,320 kWh saved/year

Category 4: Lighting - LED Retrofits.Notes: Lighting modeled at whole-home level; contractor cost based on ~$0.12/sqft × 2,500 sqft. DIY costs assume ~$7/LED bulb × 40 bulbs.
Category 4: Lighting - LED Retrofits.Installation_Cost_Methodology: Contractor-installed cost reflects average fixture swap in Atlanta; DIY assumes homeowner replacement of bulbs only.

Models.annual_kWh_savings_calculation: Assumes ~8.9% reduction of 4,500 kWh HVAC baseline = 400 kWh/year

Category 5: Attic Insulation Upgrades.Notes: Assumes typical 1,000-1,200 sqft attic, contractor-installed. HVAC load savings estimated at ~8.9% reduction (400 kWh/year from 4,500 kWh baseline) for Zone 3A climate.
Category 5: Attic Insulation Upgrades.Installation_Cost_Methodology: Costs reflect full attic coverage to DOE R-38 recommendation (Zone 3A) with blown-in cellulose, including labor/materials, light air-sealing, and equipment rental for a professional install. Assumes 1,100 sq ft attic area. Cost validated against: (1) HomeGuide overview of blown-in insulation ($900-$3,600 typical range); (2) HomeAdvisor attic insulation ranges ($1,500-$6,000, most common $1,680-$3,125 and $0.60-$2.30/sq ft); (3) Modernize attic insulation pricing ($1.50-$3.50/sq ft typical); (4) SCS Foam contractor quote of $1.70-$4.00/sq ft with air sealing; (5) Green Attic estimate of ~$3,200 for 1,000 sq ft to R-49; (6) DOE / ORNL insulation guidance confirming Zone 3A R-38 target. Selected $3,000 represents a mid-range Atlanta pro job (≈$2.70/sq ft) with light air sealing.
